frames.aligns: Mutual care among the poor; the cost of war shown.
frames.concerns: The redemption arc is joining an army and killing; revenge implied; nonresistance absent.

frames.aligns: Agency and its consequences; loyalty; a better life sought for loved ones.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth on profanity and graphic violence.

frames.aligns: The poor literally denied sunlight; corruption at the top; a capable young woman fighter.
frames.concerns: Militarism as the only exit from poverty; criminals pressed into service.

frames.aligns: A people kept under the ground long for the light (a deliverance theme); friends stand together; the lowly prove their worth.
frames.concerns: Revenge (Romans 12:19) implied and unjudged; profanity; graphic death; deliverance ends in loss rather than God making a way.

frames.aligns: Loyalty; leaving a life of crime.
frames.concerns: Violent entertainment; profanity; drinking.

frames.aligns: Loyalty and care for friends.
frames.concerns: The happy turn is military service and killing, against Witness neutrality; revenge; language.

frames.aligns: Overcoming fear; courage.
frames.concerns: Fear, death and horror as the setting.

frames.aligns: Loyalty; dignity of the poor; a corrupt official exposed.
frames.concerns: Kavod hamet: bodies devoured and a severed head shown (ch. 8); revenge; language.

frames.aligns: Friendship and responsibility; tzedek against corruption.
frames.concerns: Graphic death; revenge implied.

frames.aligns: Justice for the poor; repair through service.
frames.concerns: Violence; ends-justify-means leadership.

frames.aligns: Patience in loss (sabr); loyalty; striving against a real enemy.
frames.concerns: Revenge outside justice; profanity; alcohol.

frames.aligns: Erwin's counsel echoes acting without attachment to results (Bhagavad Gita 2:47); a warrior finds his duty.
frames.concerns: Rage and revenge rather than equanimity; violence.

frames.aligns: Impermanence and loss faced honestly; letting go of blame (ch. 8).
frames.concerns: Wrath and revenge; killing.

frames.aligns: Protecting the weak; courage; honest grief.
frames.concerns: Revenge; profanity; alcohol.

frames.aligns: Service to humanity as a whole; loyalty.
frames.concerns: Revenge and violence; alcohol.

frames.aligns: Honoring the fallen; Levi looks back at his friends' resting place (ch. 8).
frames.concerns: Death and corpses (kegare) everywhere, as genre.

frames.aligns: Longing for sky, birds and open land; loyalty.
frames.concerns: "Harm none" broken by revenge.

frames.aligns: Self-reliance and competence; overcoming a suppressive, corrupt official.
frames.concerns: Drinking; violence.

frames.aligns: Class critique (slum versus capital); corruption exposed; a capable woman fighter.
frames.concerns: The poor become soldiers; ends-justify-means leadership celebrated.

frames.aligns: Meaning made by human choice in a world without gods; knowledge of Titans as the path to freedom (ch. 8).
frames.concerns: Erwin's manipulation unexamined; violence.

frames.concerns: Graphic harm; revenge.

frames.aligns: Built on humility about outcomes: no one can know how a choice will turn out (ch. 8).
frames.concerns: Violence.

frames.aligns: Loyalty to friends; fairness against a corrupt noble; honoring the dead.
frames.concerns: Cruel deaths; a bleak middle.

frames.aligns: Discipline, duty, courage and loyalty to a commander; crime left behind.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of the poor; interdependence.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Levi answers an assault on Isabel with a knife (ch. 2) and vows to kill the man who humiliated him (ch. 2, 7).

Order vs freedom.evidence: The trio long for open sky; the ending accepts military order as the road to freedom.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Kin-like loyalty to two friends gives way to duty to humanity (ch. 8).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Rank and formation matter; criminals are looked down on (ch. 3-4); Erwin's authority wins.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Secular; knowledge of Titans is the hope (ch. 8).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival first, in the slum and outside the Walls.

folkways.japan: Loyalty to a superior who becomes a lifelong commander, Levi's obsession with cleaning (ch. 3) and the barracks discipline reflect Japanese school and workplace norms; the title's "kui naki sentaku" (a choice without regret) is a common Japanese phrase of resolve. The publication in a shōjo magazine shaped its focus on character bonds (Sean Gaffney).

delivery.evidence: The title states the theme, and Erwin speaks it at the end (ch. 8; Wikipedia OVA summary). Lovof is a flat villain; Levi's objections are given real weight before he yields.
delivery.note: The message lands in one closing speech after two chapters of loss; most of the book shows rather than tells.

personified.ideology: Loyalty to his own, then to a cause

85199.dominant: Existentialism (choice without regret), Utilitarianism (Erwin's means), Communitarianism (the trio), Stoicism.

folkways.japan: Built on Japanese yakuza film and folklore: sakazuki cups, irezumi tattoos, Kabukicho's nightlife, yokai such as oni, tanuki and kitsune (the Gyobu-Danuki legend), onmyoji exorcists and Japan's anti-yakuza ordinances. The loyalty ideal draws on these settings rather than arguing with them.

delivery.evidence: ANN notes Maruo's past is implied rather than lectured; the yakuza frame is never questioned, but Urara's revenge is (ch. 11, Doppo's charge that she did not know her father). Villains are drawn broadly (Doppo) or given reasons (Tamagawa's loyalty to his boss, ch. 23).
delivery.note: Comedy and fights carry the message; the one stated moral moment is Urara's apology and Maruo's pledge in ch. 11.

folkways.japan: Oddities draw on Japanese folk belief in kami and yōkai, shrine rituals and offerings; school hierarchy, the class president role (Hanekawa) and the third-year exam pressure frame the setting; the manga keeps the novels' Japanese wordplay that translation struggles to carry.

folkways.japan: The guests embody Japanese social problems the creators name or show: ijime (bullying), hikikomori withdrawal, a father's demand to work, study and marry, and isolation of the sick; the work borrows a Western frame (Alice, biblical imagery) to examine them.

delivery.evidence: The serpent's defense of staying (the real world is pain) is given strongly by the guests themselves (ch. 5), and Alice answers it; the twist then turns her answer against her.

30735.heading: Black Lagoon
30735.label: From summaries
30735.life_message: It holds up no settled good life: in a world without law the strong and the clever survive, but Rock's stubborn empathy argues that a person can keep some humanity, and even change others' fates for the better, without pretending the darkness away.

content.framing: Stylized and often relished as action; atrocities (torture, child killers, terror) shown as horror
Abuse condemned as the root of monsters; fan service and the sex trade shown without judgment

frames.concerns: Relativism with no moral center; the Rip-Off Church mocks religious life as a front; violence relished; Yukio's suicide (CCC 2280-2283) given tragic honor.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Roanapur has no law but the syndicates' balance; the crew answers to no one.

folkways.japan: Rock's salaryman background, his estrangement from his parents and the yakuza arc (ch. 22-37) contrast Japanese corporate conformity and giri (duty) with Roanapur's lawlessness; Yukio's honor suicide draws on Japanese tragic ideals that the story mourns rather than praises.

delivery.evidence: Rock and Revy argue morality openly (ch. 9-10, 15), and Rock and Chang argue fate and God (ch. 116); ANN's Matthew Roe says the anime rarely over-explains and leaves viewers to judge; Santos (ANN) thinks it fails to explore its controversial subjects.
delivery.note: Its question of how far an ordinary person sinks is carried by Rock's arc and by debates between characters, with no narrator or arc that settles it.

personified.ideology: Empathy and a stubborn hope for good endings
Nihilism: only money and guns protect you
Killing as the law of the world, learned through abuse

folkways.japan: A standard Japanese web-novel isekai: a reincarnated Japanese man, game status screens, a guild ranking system and a nostalgic craving for rice that leads to a Japan-like kingdom founded by earlier otherworlders (Toraj, ch. 13-22).

folkways.japan: A Japanese shōnen boarding-school comedy: senior-junior ranks, a powerful student council and prefect system, the sports festival, cultural festival, school trip, and Valentine's customs. frames.concerns: Villains often drawn as simply unreasonable (Ikemoto's own admission, Wikipedia).

frames.concerns: Frequent violence for younger readers.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Elders invoke Konoha's honour to justify killing Boruto (ch. 6); vows and vendettas (Kawaki, ch. 38); Boruto's own code is protection, not revenge.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Boruto works outside the law for the village; Shikamaru bends regulations (ch. 6); order is restored, not rejected.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Family (Himawari, his parents) and village weigh equally for Boruto; Kawaki puts family above everything.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Hokage, elders, ranks (Sarada may "stay a genin forever," ch. 1), mentors; teams treat each other as equals.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Clan powers and village customs beside science and cyborgs (Amado, ch. 18).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival against devouring enemies drives the plot; identity (Boruto's stolen name) is the other stake.

folkways.japan: The ninja village with its Hokage, council of elders and feudal lord, the master-disciple bond (Sasuke and Boruto), duty to the group and the honor of the village reflect Japanese historical and shōnen-manga norms; the Daikokuten dimension is named after a Japanese god of fortune (from general knowledge; to verify).

delivery.evidence: Ikemoto said he could not write villains with explained backstories the way Kishimoto did, so his antagonists may seem more unreasonable (Wikipedia); Kawaki and Jura, however, are given reasons and feelings (ch. 26, 38).
delivery.note: Loyalty under slander is carried by Boruto's actions rather than speeches; memory-manipulating and devouring foes stand for the opposing view.

personified.ideology: Protect the family at any cost, even by imprisoning it

168468.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (loyalty, perseverance), Communitarianism (village), Might makes right (critiqued), Transhumanism

folkways.japan: A boys' love magazine work set in a Japanese high school drama club; school clubs, a culture of not causing trouble, and onnagata-like cross-gender stage roles (my own framing; from general knowledge; to verify) shape how Arima's performance is received.

98608.heading: Campfire Cooking in Another World with My Absurd Skill
98608.label: From summaries

folkways.japan: The salaryman protagonist's politeness and caution, the love of home cooking, convenience-store and drugstore brands, bathing culture and food offerings to gods (shinsen, omiyage) are distinctly Japanese; the "slow life" isekai genre is a response to Japanese overwork culture.

delivery.evidence: The kingdom's motives are shown through Mukohda's suspicions and the fan wiki's later reveal rather than argued; Anime Feminist describes a light comedy that pokes fun at its own genre. The gods' greed is satirized but never preached against.

176740.heading: Centuria
176740.label: From summaries
176740.life_message: Kindness that treats every person as human, even a stranger, is what makes us human; a family is made by those who give themselves for a child, and that love is worth protecting against any king, god or prophecy.

content.framing: Shown with consequences; cruelty condemned, protective violence endorsed with remorse

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Julian fights to protect, not for face; but revenge and duels drive many foes (Lacrima, ch. 31-40; Ceodric's duel, ch. 84-108).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Escape from slavery and from a state that hunts a child; the village is a free, small community.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Kin by choice comes first, but Julian also repays strangers (Atoria, ch. 78-108) and sees enemies as people with families.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Slaves are shown as equals in dignity; a divine king and royal privilege are the problem.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Gods, prophecy, curses and witches are real forces in the world.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival dominates every arc; even home life is lived in hiding.

folkways.japan: A European-style fantasy (Greco-Roman, Viking and 17th-century elements, per ANN's Rebecca Silverman) drawn in the dark-fantasy line of Berserk and Vinland Saga; the found-family and self-sacrifice ideals, the guilt over surviving and the debt to the dead (Julian's hundred lives) also run through Japanese shonen storytelling.

delivery.evidence: Mira states the moral of ch. 1 aloud, but the rest is carried by events. Kill one child to save the realm

31474.heading: Devilman
31474.label: From summaries
31474.life_message: Fear and hatred of the other can make people more monstrous than demons; a loving heart is what makes someone human, and war, any war, has no justice.

folkways.japan: Written in 1972 for a boys' weekly, it blends Western demonology and Christian myth (via Dante and Doré, Nagai's childhood influences) with Japanese monster tradition; The Anime Encyclopedia found the mix of Japanese and European mythology messy (via Wikipedia). Its anti-war intent reflects the period of the Vietnam War and Cold War nuclear fear (from general knowledge; to verify).

delivery.evidence: Characters deliver long speeches on human nature and the coming end (TCJ calls it preachy; a MangaUpdates reader notes drawn-out exposition); Nagai stated the anti-war message directly (Wikipedia). The mob is shown as pure frenzy with no reasoning given (fan wiki), while Satan and the demons get reasons.
delivery.note: The warning is spoken aloud by Ryo and the narration and enacted by the mob in v5; the theology (Satan sympathetic, God as aggressor) is carried by the ending more than by argument.

The demons' right to the Earth; humans as the true destroyers
Fear and hatred of anyone different

folkways.japan: The samurai code, the Shinsengumi and the Bakumatsu-era unequal treaties, the senpai and teacher bond (sensei), Edo nostalgia, Kabuki-cho nightlife and Shonen Jump fan culture are Japanese material that the series both honors and parodies; Gintoki's personal code is a modern reworking of bushido.

delivery.evidence: Sorachi describes the series as gently portraying a loser's life and a likeable humanity (Wikipedia, Hideaki Sorachi); serious arcs state the code through Gintoki's actions between gag chapters.
delivery.note: The personal code is shown more than preached; villains like Takasugi and Kamui get their reasons, though tyrants such as Housen are flat.

folkways.japan: Post-disaster Japan after earthquakes and tsunamis, Kojiki myth names, school life, and Ishiguro's unease about Japanese governance before the 2020 Olympics shape the setting (Wikipedia); the gender theme is written against Japanese manga's tradition of comic body-swaps.

folkways.japan: A European-styled fantasy setting (MangaUpdates: European Ambience) built on Japanese yuri conventions (the dormitory, roommates, an all-girl school) and the postwar Japanese anti-war tradition of child-soldier stories; it draws on those conventions while turning them toward grief.

folkways.japan: The overlooked salaryman father, an aging society, the hikikomori (Naoyuki), bullying, 2channel-style anonymous boards and media scrums, yakuza syndicates and Japan's SAT police unit reflect modern Japanese settings and anxieties; Ichiro's flight to the Astro Boy theme pays tribute to Osamu Tezuka.

delivery.evidence: The two cyborgs openly embody opposite answers to what makes someone human, and say so (Wikipedia eps. 7, 10; TV Tropes). Thompson calls it an idealistic superhero story played straight. Hiro is given motives (his mother, Shion) and a final sacrifice rather than drawn as a pure monster.
delivery.note: The message is carried by action and by the mirror between the two leads; there are few speeches but no ambiguity about which path is right.

198372.heading: Jujutsu Kaisen Modulo
198372.label: From summaries
198372.life_message: Living as neighbors with people who are strange to you takes patience, listening and sacrifice; peace is made by people willing to lose rather than win the wrong way, and the old cycle of fear and revenge can be ended.

content.framing: Mixed: battle action shown as thrilling; cruelty and murder condemned; one revenge killing approved
Shown with consequences; sacrifice honored and then undone

frames.concerns: Sorcery, shikigami and a cursed ring as the heroes' tools (CCC 2117 on magic); a ritual that rewrites human souls; Dabura's revenge beheading left unjudged (ch. 24).

frames.aligns: Peacemaking over vengeance; Usami offers his life for his people (ch. 13); reverence for the sacred respected (ch. 7, 25).
frames.concerns: Curses and spirits worked by sorcerers as real powers; Maru's ritual remakes souls, a power the tradition reserves to God; violence.

frames.aligns: Love for the outsider (Leviticus 19:34); evil men who sell children punished; sibling devotion and sacrifice.
frames.concerns: Sorcery and curses at the core (Deuteronomy 18:10-12); a soul-altering ritual saves the day; battle violence and a severed head (ch. 24).

frames.aligns: Hospitality to aliens and refugees opens talk about neighbor love; Tsurugi's humility; no mockery of faith.
frames.concerns: Heroes wield curses and shikigami, beyond Tolkien-style magic for many families; salvation by a technique, not by grace.

frames.aligns: Resisting hatred between peoples; protecting children from exploiters.
frames.concerns: Curses, possessing spirits (Rika in the ring, ch. 17-18), a soul-eating curse (Mahito, ch. 22) and sacred beasts worshipped for millennia are the world's core, not background.

frames.aligns: Civil authority used carefully for peace (Romans 13); human dignity across peoples; sin shown in fear and greed (ch. 9, 13).
frames.concerns: Occult framework; a humanly engineered remaking of souls as the answer; justice by duel.

frames.aligns: Two-kingdoms themes: diplomats, councils and sorcerers each claim authority; vocation as service (Usami, Mino).
frames.concerns: Curse-based powers; Dabura's revenge killing approved; violence.

frames.aligns: Social holiness: building a just peace for displaced people; works of mercy (Yuka and Cross with a lost child, ch. 7).
frames.concerns: Violence as the way disputes are settled (duels); occult framing of powers.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Duels of champions and a warrior's code settle disputes (ch. 9, 13); Dabura's revenge restores his people's honor (ch. 24); heroes also choose humility over face (ch. 21).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Careful rules and diplomacy are honored, but cover-ups are criticized and Yuji acts on his own (ch. 12, 20).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Sibling love drives the heroes; the larger aim is peace with strangers.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Clan inheritance, ranked sorcerers and a men-only warrior caste exist; the story gently questions each (ch. 1, 11, 12).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Rituals and sacred beasts are respected; diplomacy, votes and science-fiction technology sit beside them.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: A war for living space and resources frames the plot; personal wishes (Yuka's ring, Maru's amusement park) are small but real.

folkways.japan: Clan inheritance (the Gojo and Zen'in families), deference to elders and committees, a government that manages public fear, Japan's postwar stance on nuclear weapons (ch. 14) and the memory of hidden Christians and the fumi-e (ch. 7) reflect Japanese settings; the refugee theme reads, in a French critic's view, as an echo of Japan's own debates over immigration.

delivery.evidence: Dura states the neighbor ideal in a speech (ch. 9); the pro-war Osuki and the fearful Yakumaru are drawn thinly, but Cross's resentment and Dabura's code get real backstories (ch. 8-9, 18).
delivery.note: The coexistence theme is argued through characters on both sides and a vote, not lectures; the final peace comes by a supernatural ritual rather than persuasion.

folkways.japan: Elite private schools, student councils with real power, family clans (the Hundred Devouring Families) and the shame of debt reflect Japanese settings; gambling for money is illegal in Japan outside licensed forms, so the academy is a fantasy of what money can do (from general knowledge; to verify).

delivery.evidence: Yumeko explains each cheat and sometimes lectures her opponents on why rigged games are pointless (CBR on her sportsmanship); villains like Kiwatari are cartoon bullies, while Kirari, Midari and Sayaka get motives.

folkways.japan: A Japanese shonen reimagining of Victorian Britain: the "gentleman" villain and "rough" detective (Wikipedia, Production), intense bonds between brothers and rivals, and a hero who takes the nation's sins on himself. Dignity vs honor.evidence: Nezumi's grudge against the city for his people, tempered by Shion's insistence on mercy (ch. 3, 27).

folkways.japan: Shion's polite, sheltered upbringing set against Nezumi's outsider bluntness plays on Japanese inside-outside (uchi-soto) distinctions; the forest people and their goddess echo Japanese ideas of nature spirits; the story's anti-war, anti-state tone fits much postwar Japanese youth fiction.

delivery.evidence: ANN's vol. 9 review: much of the final volume explains the city's truth, though the reviewer found it seldom reads as an info-dump. delivery.note: The critique of the controlled city is carried by the plot and, in the last volumes, by long explanation of the city's secrets.

folkways.japan: A seinen workplace drama: a low-status section inside a big corporation, a son measured against a famous father, a mother's promise that he come home alive, and nods to Miyazawa Kenji, whose Guskou Budori gives his life for others (v4). The cast is international (Russian, American, Japanese, Middle Eastern), and the story's values of humility, work and family sit comfortably with Japanese norms.

86526.label: From summaries

folkways.japan: Japan's high youth suicide rate, abuse in foster care by relatives, school bullying and the media's role in public judgment all shape the story; the God and angels are borrowed Western imagery rather than Japanese religion.

delivery.evidence: Candidates state their philosophies on national television (hedonism, euthanasia, leisure, happiness, unbelief; ch. 37-41) and Mirai and Yoneda debate at length (v12-13); Metropoliman is drawn as a cartoonish villain, but Yoneda and Shuji get serious hearings.

folkways.japan: School bullying (ijime), adults and teachers who look away, a local political dynasty with yakuza ties, and cremation-centered funerals reflect Japanese settings; the slasher form, the Halloween party and the social-media stalking draw on American horror films, which the fan wiki traces to Carrie, Scream and Friday the 13th.

delivery.evidence: The bullies and the Kuroki family are drawn as almost wholly cruel or selfish (Naruto kills his own friend to stay safe); Kazuya and Detective Matsui are the only figures with mixed views.
delivery.note: The message is carried by horror set pieces and dark humor (AniList: Surreal Comedy), not by speeches; Naoko's confrontations and Naruto's forced live-stream confession (ch. 14) state the moral case.

folkways.japan: The Bakumatsu and early Meiji era: the 1876 sword ban, ex-samurai turned police or bandits, the Shinsengumi, the anti-Buddhist movement after 1868 and the Meiji state's suppression of the Sekiho Army. Japanese readers met an optimistic, revisionist picture of samurai (Wikipedia); the story draws on the warrior ideal but sets its hero against the killing at its core.

delivery.evidence: Kenshin states his vow and its reasons often, but Saito's and Shishio's creeds are given strong voices and are never simply mocked; Saito is left standing (Beneath the Tangles, 2015; fan wiki).
delivery.note: The anti-killing, anti-revenge message is carried by plot tests and speeches in the duels; Watsuki said redemption came from the shojo manga he grew up on (Wikipedia).

folkways.japan: Senpai-kohai relationships, club life, school and summer festivals (ch. 31, vol. 8) and the Japanese yuri tradition, including Class S stories of devoted schoolgirl friendship that Yori finds in vol. 4 (ANN), shape the setting; the series moves from that tradition toward open, mutual couples.

folkways.japan: Draws on the Japanese yankee (delinquent) genre, which the English vol. 1 translation notes explain, and on the shotengai, the covered neighborhood shopping street. Senpai-kohai ranks, a "Four Heavenly Kings" leadership and the guardian idea fit Japanese conventions; the story recasts delinquents as a neighborhood watch.

delivery.evidence: Bofurin's creed is stated by Kotoha (ch. 1), Umemiya and the recited motto (fan wiki); Natori is drawn as a sadist with no sympathetic side, while Shishitoren, GRAVEL and Noroshi get backstories (fan wiki).

folkways.japan: Ayakashi and yokai lore, Shinto and Buddhist imagery, seasonal customs, the idea of fated connection, and the household of mistress and servant reflect Japanese folk belief and settings; the art borrows from ukiyo-e (Wikipedia). Dignity vs honor.evidence: Toguro's honor code, fair duels, and Mukuro's endorsed revenge (v19) lean to honor; Yusuke's mercy and Kurama's restraint lean to dignity.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Yusuke ignores rules and orders; the corrupt order of Spirit World is overturned (ch. 175); Genkai's discipline is honored.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Friends and family come first (Kurama's mother; Keiko), but the team also saves the whole human world.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Demon Plane ranks by class (A, S) and power; Spirit World's hierarchy; Yusuke flattens both at the end with an open tournament.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: An afterlife, spirits and old martial traditions are real within the story; no science-based answers.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Battles for survival alongside a delinquent's self-assertion and later a ramen stand and a proposal (ch. 171-175).

folkways.japan: The delinquent (yankī) hero, the old martial-arts master, a Buddhist-style afterlife with King Enma and the Sanzu River, yokai, and Weekly Shonen Jump's tournament structure reflect Japanese settings and genre norms; the story's respect for teachers and its distrust of a lying authority sit side by side.

delivery.evidence: Sensui's case against humanity is shown through the Chapter Black tape and the Feast of Human Vices rather than dismissed; Toguro's code is respected even as he loses; the rich patrons are drawn as cartoon villains.
delivery.note: The moral is carried by actions in fights and by a few quiet scenes (the wake, Toguro's sentencing, Sensui's death) rather than speeches.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Challenges must be fought and Brago's honorable duel is respected (ch. 321), but the kind king ideal rejects feuds and revenge.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The tournament has fixed rules set by the mamodo world; partners choose freely how to fight.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Loyalty to partner and allies; Zatch's royal family and his twin are central (ch. 259-275).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: A contest for a throne, yet the kind king ideal raises the weakest; Zatch goes back to ordinary school as king (fan wiki, ch. 322-323).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Monarchy and magic beside a modern Japanese school and a scientist father.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival battles, but character, trust and friendship matter most.

folkways.japan: Kiyo's isolation as a gifted student who stands out reflects Japanese school pressure against standing out; the story prizes group harmony, loyal friendship and a gentle ruler, and the shōnen tournament format of rivals who become allies.

delivery.evidence: Thompson (ANN) says the early chapters hammer the self-esteem and friendship messages through shouting and repetition, easing later; the villains are rotten enough to cheer against, but Zeno and Koko are redeemed.
delivery.note: The kind-king message is spoken aloud in battle and repeated, especially early, but carried by big emotional scenes rather than lectures.

act-age.weigh: a teenage girl raising her siblings after her mother's death, refusing her absent father's money (ch. 1-5); good mentors who protect a gifted young person (Kuroyama, Iwao); a warning about losing oneself in a role and the breakdown it once caused (Arisa); a dying director's last work and funeral (ch. 36-53); rivalry that becomes respect (Kei and Chiyoko); a producer who tries to sell Kei's tragedy (ch. 54-62); almost no violence, sex, drinking or profanity. The series is unfinished. The writer's 2020 conviction for indecent acts against two middle-school girls ended it; this is real-world context, not part of the story's message, and is not graded.

Seven Seas rates the manga Teen 13+; Common Sense Media rates the anime 14+.

bibliomania.weigh: a story that condemns escapism and false paradises: every guest who stays in a wish-world is consumed; a serpent tempter with 666 guests and biblical words in its mouth; bullying, addiction, a family's neglect and a suicide attempt, all told as the guests' wounds; heavy body and cosmic horror; a twist in which the heroine is the monster that devoured the world through an insatiable hunger for knowledge, and an ending with no redemption. No scene sexualizing a minor was found in sources opened.

high-rise-invasion.weigh: a survival story whose heroine refuses despair and will not abandon her friends; a manufactured 'God' system that makes ordinary people kill or push others to suicide, condemned and partly defeated; heroes who survive by killing brainwashed people, sometimes brutally; constant forced suicides; an attempted sexual assault on a high-school girl that is stopped and punished (ch. 9-10); recurring fan service of teenage girls (panty shots, torn clothing) for the reader; a same-sex crush (Mayuko for Yuri) shown sympathetically; an ending where the system survives. **Content involving minors:** sexualized framing of high-school characters recurs from vol. 1 onward, and an adult attempts to sexually assault Yuri, a minor (ch. 9-10); Kuon (16) is said to have fled an attempted assault (ch. 50).

A MyAnimeList reviewer warns the series shows rape, child sexual abuse and child abuse graphically; how much is shown on the page has not been checked (see checklist).

mushishi.weigh: a gentle, episodic story of a wandering healer who treats every living thing with respect and seeks understanding rather than blame; a spirit-like natural world (mushi, a life force beneath the land, a mountain's guardian, rebirth in ch. 21) presented as nature rather than gods; tragedies accepted rather than undone (ch. 3, 13); a village's hidden bargain of one life per harvest (ch. 13); eerie body horror without gore; the hero's constant smoking; no sexual content, profanity or violence of note reported. No scene sexualizing a minor was found in sources opened.

ouran-high-school-host-club.weigh: a heroine who values honesty, study and frugality over wealth and status; a parody of flirtation and boys'-love tropes in which the hosts' romance is a performance; a crossdressing father shown as a loving parent, and other gender-nonconforming characters accepted; the twins' staged incest-themed flirting for customers, which the story outgrows as the twins seek independence; a family reconciliation won by honesty and Tamaki's patience with a cold grandmother (ch. 72-81); a chaste romance that ends in a couple (ch. 80-83); dated terms for Ranka in some translations and a stereotyped all-female club. rurouni-kenshin.weigh: a former assassin's lifelong atonement through a vow never to kill again (throughout); mercy shown to defeated enemies and redemption arcs for Megumi, Aoshi, Sojiro and Anji; revenge rejected (v18-27); the 'strong rule the weak' creed defeated (v13-17); constant sword violence, bloody in the assassin flashback (ch. 165-179); a found family and a marriage at the end (v28); a crossdressing villain and a courtesan lover treated with some dignity; a fallen Buddhist monk and a comic scene in Buddhist hell (v17); opium condemned; two suicides or attempts among villains (v15, v17). No scene sexualizing a minor was reported; see the checklist on Kenshin and Tomoe's married life in the flashback (Kenshin about 15). Some readers weigh the creator's 2018 conviction (Creator context) when deciding whether to buy.

terra-formars.weigh: extreme gore in nearly every chapter; heroes who die so others can live (vol. 1; Mars finale); governments and a secret society that use people as tools, condemned; betrayals by Victoria Wood, Hiruma, the Chinese squad and Joseph Newton; a eugenic clan; female characters' backstories of sexual abuse and captive women forced to bear hybrids (Earth saga), condemned; a drug injected for power; Bible plague passages at heroic last stands; evolution and "survival of the fittest" as the story's science; and three reviewers' concern that the Terraformars' design echoes racist caricatures of Black people (ANN; Sequential State; Manga Bookshelf). A backstory of sexual abuse of Nanao by her stepfather (vol. 1; age not stated in sources opened) and a mention of genital cutting at age 12 in Victoria's backstory (vol. 1) are stated, not described further in sources.
